files.lesson.md: --- order: 9 unit: pythagoras node: AC9M8M06 n1 uses: [AC9M7N01 n2, AC9M7SP02 n1] # squares and square roots; right-angled triangles title: Pythagoras' theorem summary: "Draw a square on each side of a right-angled triangle. The two smaller squares together have exactly the same area as the biggest: a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse, the side opposite the right angle." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Every lawn has one: the worn path straight across the corner, where people skip the footpath. How much does it save?" connection: grass-shortcut # data/connections/maths.yml (opening situation and Make; documentation only) app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8284 url: http://127.0.0.1:8284/index.html readySelector: "#sl-b" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: tri.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Squares on the sides of a 3-4-5 right-angled triangle: $9 + 16 = 25$. The two smaller squares exactly make the biggest." } explainClip: query: { code: "@tri.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Squares on the sides" say: "Draw a square on each side." clip: - caption: { text: "Sides 3 and 3 at the right angle: 9 + 9 = 18.", say: "Sides three and three: nine and nine make eighteen." } - wait: 1200 - caption: { text: "Make b = 4: 9 + 16 = 25, the big square exactly.", say: "Make one side four. Nine and sixteen make twenty-five." } - click: Make side b longer - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "= 5²" } - wait: 600 - caption: { text: "a² + b² = c², so c = √25 = 5.", say: "So the long side is the square root: five." } - wait: 1200 --- The footpath round this corner of the lawn is 24 m one way and 10 m the other, so 34 m in all. People cut straight across the grass instead. How long is the shortcut, and how much does it save? Have a guess, and we'll come back to it at the end. The two footpaths and the shortcut make a right-angled triangle, and the shortcut is its longest side. How is that side linked to the other two? In a right-angled triangle, the longest side is opposite the right angle. It is called the **hypotenuse**, $c$. The two sides that meet at the right angle are $a$ and $b$. **Pythagoras' theorem** says that the squares on the two shorter sides add up to the square on the hypotenuse: $$a^2 + b^2 = c^2$$ To find the hypotenuse: square the two shorter sides, add, then take the square root. ## Predict: sides 3 and 4 ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a hypotenuse for legs 3 and 4 shows whether they add the sides (7), add the squares without rooting (25), or expect 5." check: type: predict q: "A right-angled triangle has sides 3 cm and 4 cm at the right angle. How long is the hypotenuse?" options: ["5 cm", "7 cm", "25 cm", "12 cm"] actual: "5 cm. 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5². Adding the sides (7) is too long: the straight route across is shorter than going round the corner." ``` Is the hypotenuse shorter or longer than going round the corner, 3 + 4? ## Run: squares on the sides ```step stage: run insight: "Building a 3-4-5 triangle with squares on its sides shows the two small squares' areas add exactly to the big one." try: { playground: board, starter: "tri.yml#run", height: 620 } check: { type: board, text: "Make a = 3 and b = 4. Do the two smaller squares add up to the biggest? Was your prediction right?", when: "a = 3 and b = 4", explain: "9 + 16 = 25: the biggest square, so c = 5 cm." } ``` Count the unit squares in each square, or read the numbers inside them. ## Investigate: square, add, root ```step stage: investigate insight: "Square both shorter sides, add, then root; Leah adds the sides, which is always too long. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "A right-angled triangle has sides 12 cm and 16 cm at the right angle. How long is the hypotenuse, in cm?" answer: "20" feedback: - ["28", "That adds the sides. Square them first: 144 + 256."] - ["400", "That is c². Take the square root."] explain: "12² + 16² = 144 + 256 = 400, so c = √400 = 20 cm." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#leah" text: "Leah finds the hypotenuse. Click the line where her method goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: pyth-no-squares explain: "Line 2: it is the squares that add: 36 + 64 = 100, so c = 10 cm. 14 cm would be longer than going round the corner." - check: type: question q: "Which side of a right-angled triangle is the hypotenuse?" options: ["The side opposite the right angle, the longest", "The side along the bottom", "Either side at the right angle", "The shortest side"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Triangles can be turned any way: it depends on the right angle, not the bottom.", "Those are a and b.", "The hypotenuse is always the longest."] explain: "The hypotenuse faces the right angle and is always the longest side." ``` ### Square, add, root Here is the method. ```worked c \text{ is opposite the right angle} :: Find the hypotenuse first. a^2 + b^2 = 6^2 + 8^2 = 36 + 64 = 100 :: Square the two shorter sides and add. c = \sqrt{100} = 10 \text{ cm} :: Take the square root. 6 < 10 < 6 + 8 :: Check: longer than each shorter side, shorter than both together. ``` Now try one: sides 12 cm and 16 cm. ### Find the mistake Read Leah's working. Which is shorter: across or round the corner? ### The hypotenuse ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: another whole-number triangle on the board, a new pair of sides, a hypotenuse that is not a whole number, then why the hypotenuse is always the longest." try: { playground: board, starter: "tri.yml#twelve", height: 620 } tasks: - starter: "tri.yml#twelve" hint: "Set a = 5 and b = 12, then read the biggest square and c." check: { type: board, text: "Make a right-angled triangle with sides 5 and 12 at the right angle. How long is the hypotenuse?", when: "a = 5 and b = 12", explain: "25 + 144 = 169 = 13²: c = 13." } - check: type: answer q: "The sides at the right angle are 9 m and 12 m. How long is the hypotenuse, in m?" answer: "15" feedback: - ["21", "That adds the sides."] - ["225", "That is c². Take the square root."] explain: "81 + 144 = 225, √225 = 15 m." - check: type: number q: "The sides at the right angle are both 1 m. How long is the hypotenuse, in m, to two decimal places?" answer: 1.41 tolerance: 0.005 explain: "1 + 1 = 2, so c = √2 ≈ 1.41 m: between 1 and 2, as it must be." - check: type: question q: "Edge case: why is the hypotenuse always the longest side?" options: ["c² = a² + b² is bigger than a² and bigger than b²", "It is always drawn longest", "Because it is at the bottom"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Drawings can mislead; the theorem decides.", "The hypotenuse can point any way."] explain: "c² is a² plus something, so c² > a², and c > a; the same for b." ``` ### 5 and 12 Each task changes one thing. ### 9 and 12 ### Not a whole number ### Always the longest ## Practise: the hypotenuse ```step stage: practise insight: "Whole-number and decimal hypotenuses and a real context, mixed; adding the sides is the planted slip; the review keeps square roots fresh." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "The sides at the right angle are 8 cm and 15 cm. Hypotenuse, in cm?" answer: "17" feedback: - ["23", "That adds the sides."] - ["289", "That is c²: take the square root."] explain: "64 + 225 = 289, √289 = 17 cm." - check: type: number q: "The sides at the right angle are 2 cm and 3 cm. Hypotenuse, in cm, to two decimal places?" answer: 3.61 tolerance: 0.005 explain: "4 + 9 = 13, √13 ≈ 3.61 cm." - check: type: answer q: "A park is a rectangle 30 m by 40 m. How long is the path straight across, corner to corner, in m?" answer: "50" feedback: - ["70", "That is walking round two sides."] explain: "The diagonal is a hypotenuse: 900 + 1600 = 2500, √2500 = 50 m." smaller: check: { type: "question", q: "Which length is the hypotenuse, the side across from the right angle?", options: ["The path from corner to corner", "The 40 m side", "The 30 m side"], answer: 0, explain: "The right angle is at the corner of the park, and the path across doesn't touch it. So the path is the hypotenuse." } - check: type: answer q: "Review: work out $\\sqrt{144}$." answer: "12" feedback: - ["72", "That is half of 144."] explain: "12 × 12 = 144." ``` ### 8 and 15 ### A decimal ### A shortcut across ### Review: roots ## Make: back to the shortcut ```step stage: make insight: "Coming back to the opening question: the shortcut is the hypotenuse of the two footpaths, and the saving is what makes the answer mean something." tasks: - hint: ["The two footpaths are the sides at the right angle.", "24² + 10² = 576 + 100."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "The footpaths round the corner are 24 m and 10 m. How long is the shortcut straight across the grass, in m?" steps: - ["The shortcut is the hypotenuse", "the footpaths meet at a right angle, and the shortcut is opposite it"] - ["$c^2 = 24^2 + 10^2 = 576 + 100 = 676$", "for the hypotenuse, add the squares"] - ["$c = \\sqrt{676} = 26$ m", "take the square root"] criteria: - "I sketched the corner and marked the right angle." - "I squared, added, then took the square root." - "My shortcut is shorter than the 34 m round the corner." answer: "26" feedback: - ["34", "That is the footpath round the corner. The shortcut is shorter: square, add, then take the square root."] - ["676", "That is the square on the shortcut. Take the square root."] - ["14", "That subtracts the sides. The squares add: 576 + 100."] explain: "24² + 10² = 576 + 100 = 676, and √676 = 26 m." - check: type: answer q: "How much shorter is the shortcut than the footpath, in m?" answer: "8" feedback: - ["26", "That is the shortcut itself. Compare it with the 34 m round the corner."] - ["10", "That is one footpath. Take the shortcut from the whole way round, 34 m."] explain: "34 − 26 = 8 m. On a 34 m walk that is about a quarter saved, which is why the path gets worn." ``` ### The shortcut Back to the lawn from the start. On paper, sketch the triangle and mark the right angle before you work anything out. ### What it saves Stretch: on a board, make a right-angled triangle with whole-number sides whose longest side is exactly 10. Is it a new triangle, or 3-4-5 made bigger? **Also used in** - **Screen sizes.** A TV or phone is sold by its diagonal, the longest side of the screen. Will it fit the cabinet? - **Ladders.** How high up a wall a ladder reaches, when you know its length and how far out its foot is (next lesson). - **Square corners.** Builders check a corner with a 3-4-5 triangle of string: the theorem run backwards (two lessons on). ```teacher summary: Students build right-angled triangles with squares on each side, see that the two smaller squares exactly make the biggest, and use a² + b² = c² to find the hypotenuse (AC9M8M06, node 1). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can find the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle. - I can explain Pythagoras' theorem with squares on the sides. - I can check that an answer is sensible (longer than each short side, shorter than both together). struggle: Keeping the order square, add, root. Ask students to say the three steps before they touch a calculator, and to check the answer against the two shorter sides. before: > Pilot (Oct 2026): the lesson opens with a real question (how much does the worn shortcut across a lawn save?) and Make comes back to it; "Also used in" closes it. The middle of the lesson is unchanged. Tell us whether the opening helps or gets in the way. Do the Run board yourself first. Students need squares and square roots (Number Foundations) and right-angled triangles (Classifying triangles). The one idea: the areas of the squares on the two shorter sides add to the area of the square on the hypotenuse. The common mistake is adding the sides (Leah's mistake). The sense check (between the longer short side and the sum) catches most slips. This is the curriculum's Year 8 content; it is placed here, after circles, because it needs Year 7 squares and roots and triangle names. running: - "Predict: take a vote; students who chose 7 added; 25 forgot the root." - "Run: count the small squares in the 9 and 16 and see the 25 together." - "Investigate: write 'square, add, root' on the board." - "Modify: for √2, ask between which whole numbers it lies before computing." - "Make: back to the shortcut across the grass. Ask for a guess at the saving before anyone calculates (most guess too much); then ask why the path gets worn even though it saves only 8 m." - "Paper: the shortcut in Make is worked on paper; the page marks only the answer and then shows a model to compare. Books out, and look at the sketches." stuck: - see: A student adds the sides (Leah's mistake). ask: Is walking across shorter or longer than going round the corner? fix: Square both, add, then root. - see: A student stops at c² (25 for 3 and 4). ask: Is 25 a length or an area? fix: "It is the big square's area: root it for the side." - see: A student cannot tell which side is the hypotenuse. ask: Where is the right angle? Which side does not touch it? fix: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle. stretch: Find three more whole-number triangles (Pythagorean triples) that are not multiples of 3-4-5. support: Use squared paper for the squares; keep a list of squares to 20² visible. leads: > Next: Finding a side (node 2), including a shorter side. Where it leads: distance between points on a graph, trigonometry (Year 10), and 3D diagonals. exit: q: A right-angled triangle has sides 10 cm and 24 cm at the right angle. Find the hypotenuse. a: 100 + 576 = 676, √676 = 26 cm. explain: > In a right-angled triangle, the **hypotenuse** $c$ is the side opposite the right angle (the longest). **Pythagoras' theorem**: the squares on the two shorter sides add to the square on the hypotenuse, $$a^2 + b^2 = c^2$$ To find $c$: square $a$ and $b$, add, then take the square root. With 6 and 8: $36 + 64 = 100$, $c = 10$. ```

A right-angled triangle has shorter sides 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the hypotenuse.

6 + 8 = 14
